subtopics.title: Line parallel to a plane, or in a plane
subtopics.theory_md:
First angle: FV above xy, TV below xy; a point $x$ above HP and $y$ in front of VP gives $a'$ at $x$ above and $a$ at $y$ below xy.

- Line **parallel to HP**: FV $\parallel xy$; TV is the **true length** and shows the true $\phi$ to VP.
- Line **parallel to VP**: TV $\parallel xy$; FV is the true length and shows the true $\theta$ to HP.
- Parallel to both: both views $\parallel xy$, true length.
- **Traces**: HT is where the line meets HP, VT where it meets VP. A line parallel to HP has **no HT**; parallel to VP has **no VT**.
- To find a trace, extend one view to xy and project to the other view.
subtopics.basics_md: A view is true length when the line is parallel to the plane that view is drawn on. The FV is the picture on the VP, the TV the picture on the HP. If the line is flat to the HP, the TV is its honest size.
key_points: Parallel to HP: FV $\parallel xy$, TV = true length at $\phi$
Parallel to VP: TV $\parallel xy$, FV = true length at $\theta$
No HT if parallel to HP; no VT if parallel to VP
Trace: extend a view to xy, project to the other view

questions.q: A 50 mm line PQ is parallel to the HP and inclined at $30^\circ$ to the VP. End P is 15 mm above the HP and 20 mm in front of the VP. Draw the projections and find the traces.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Data.** Parallel to HP so TV = 50 mm true length at $\phi=30^\circ$; FV $\parallel xy$.

1. Mark $p'$ 15 mm above xy, $p$ 20 mm below xy on one projector.
2. Draw $pq = 50$ mm at $30^\circ$ to xy (away from xy).
3. FV: $p'q'$ is $\parallel xy$, 15 mm above, length $50\cos30^\circ = 43.30$ mm.
4. Q is $20 + 50\sin30^\circ = 45$ mm in front of VP.
5. **HT:** does not exist.
6. **VT:** extend $qp$ to xy; the point is $20/25 = 0.8$ of the way, so $v'$ is 15 mm above xy, $0.8\times43.30 = 34.64$ mm from $p'$ on the side away from Q.

FV length 43.30 mm
Q is 45 mm in front of VP
HT does not exist
VT located by extending TV to xy and projecting up to the FV line at 15 mm

subtopics.title: Line inclined to both planes: true angles given
subtopics.theory_md:
For a line of length $L$ at true inclinations $\theta$ (HP) and $\phi$ (VP):

- **TV $=L\cos\theta$**, **FV $=L\cos\phi$**.
- Height difference $=L\sin\theta$; difference in distance from VP $=L\sin\phi$.
- Always $\theta+\phi\le90^\circ$.

**Steps (rotating line):** (1) draw the line parallel to VP at $\theta$: FV $a'b_1'=L$, TV $ab_1=L\cos\theta$; (2) rotate $ab_1$ about $a$ through $\phi$ to $ab$ (arc to the locus of $b$); (3) project $b$ up to the horizontal locus of $b_1'$ to get $b'$.

Traces then as before.
subtopics.basics_md: Draw the line first as if it only tilts up (HP angle). Then spin the plan view about its end until the VP angle is right. Spinning changes where B sits sideways but not its height.
key_points: TV $=L\cos\theta$, FV $=L\cos\phi$
Rise $=L\sin\theta$, depth change $=L\sin\phi$
$\theta+\phi\le90^\circ$ or data are impossible
Rotate TV about the fixed end; height is unchanged by this rotation

subtopics.title: Line given by end positions or by view lengths
subtopics.theory_md:
**Ends given** (heights, distances, projector gap $x$): plot both views directly. True length by rotation or the trapezoid method:
$$TL=\sqrt{x^2+\Delta h^2+\Delta d^2},\quad \sin\theta=\Delta h/TL,\quad \sin\phi=\Delta d/TL$$
**Views given** (FV and TV lengths): $\cos\theta=TV/L$, $\cos\phi=FV/L$; with a point and one angle use $FV=L\cos\phi$ or $TV=L\cos\theta$.

**Traces** by similar triangles: HT lies where height reaches 0, i.e. a fraction $h_A/\Delta h$ back from A; VT where distance reaches 0, a fraction $d_A/\Delta d$ back. Project: extend FV to xy for HT, extend TV to xy for VT.
subtopics.basics_md: The data are a coordinate dot-to-dot: three differences (along, up, in/out) describe the line completely. The true length is just 3-D Pythagoras.
key_points: $TL=\sqrt{x^2+\Delta h^2+\Delta d^2}$; $\sin\theta=\Delta h/TL$, $\sin\phi=\Delta d/TL$
If views are given: $\cos\theta=TV/L$, $\cos\phi=FV/L$
HT: extend FV to xy, drop to TV; VT: extend TV to xy, rise to FV
State HT as distance in front or behind VP, VT as distance above or below HP

questions.q: A line AB has A 20 mm above HP and 15 mm in front of VP, B 50 mm above HP and 60 mm in front of VP. The projectors are 40 mm apart. Find true length, inclinations and the traces.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Differences:** $x=40$, $\Delta h=30$, $\Delta d=45$ mm.

**True length:** $TL=\sqrt{40^2+30^2+45^2}=\sqrt{4525}=67.27$ mm

**Inclinations:** $\theta=\sin^{-1}(30/67.27)=26.49^\circ$, $\phi=\sin^{-1}(45/67.27)=41.99^\circ$

**Construction:** draw $a'b'$ and $ab$ from the coordinates; rotate $ab$ parallel to xy and project to get TL and $\theta$; rotate $a'b'$ for $\phi$.

**HT:** height 20 reaches 0 at $20/30=2/3$ back from A: $26.67$ mm along xy from $a'$, depth $15-45\times\frac23=-15$, so **15 mm behind VP**.

**VT:** depth 15 reaches 0 at $15/45=1/3$ back: $13.33$ mm from $a'$, height $20-30/3=10$, so **10 mm above HP**.

subtopics.title: True length in rooms, cubes and shortest distances
subtopics.theory_md:
Real-life points are located as ($x$ along, $y$ from the wall = distance from VP, $z$ above floor = height above HP). The shortest distance between two points is the **true length** of the line joining them.

Space diagonal of a room $a\times b\times c$ or cube: $\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$ ($s\sqrt3$ for a cube).

Graphically: the TV of the diagonal is the floor diagonal; the FV is the elevation. Rotate the TV parallel to xy and project up, or build a right triangle on the TV with the height difference ($\Delta h$) as the other leg; the hypotenuse is the TL. Use a scale, e.g. 1 cm = 1 m.
subtopics.basics_md: A room is a box with a floor (HP) and a back wall (VP). The straight distance between two spots is the length of a string pulled tight; the views are its shadows on the floor and wall.
key_points: Locate each point as ($x$, distance from VP, height)
TV of a space diagonal is the floor diagonal
TL by right triangle: base = TV, height = $\Delta h$
Cube diagonal $=s\sqrt3$; check by formula

questions.why: $\sqrt{s^2+s^2+s^2}=s\sqrt3$; $s\sqrt2$ is a face diagonal.

questions.q: A room is 6 m x 5 m x 4 m high. Find graphically the distance between a top corner and the diagonally opposite bottom corner. Check by calculation.

2. Draw the elevation $6\times4$ above xy; $a'$ is 4 m above xy, $b'$ on xy.
3. Rotate $ab$ parallel to xy and project to the height of $a'$; the joining line is the TL.

**Check:** $TL=\sqrt{6^2+5^2+4^2}=\sqrt{77}=8.77$ m.

subtopics.title: Plane perpendicular to one plane, inclined to the other
subtopics.theory_md:
A plane **perpendicular to HP and inclined $\phi$ to VP**: its TV is a **line** inclined $\phi$ to xy (true width), the FV is the shape with widths cut by $\cos\phi$ and heights true.

A plane **perpendicular to VP and inclined $\theta$ to HP**: FV is a line at $\theta$ (true height), TV has depths cut by $\cos\theta$.

**Two stages.** (1) Plane parallel to the plane where its true shape is drawn; the other view is a line parallel to xy. (2) Tilt that line to the given angle about the edge or point on xy; project the other view.

A plane $\perp$ VP resting on an edge has that edge $\perp$ VP. Traces: the FV line is the VT; HT is $\perp$ xy through where the VT meets xy.
subtopics.basics_md: Stand a card upright (perpendicular to the floor): from above you see it as a line. Turn it about its vertical edge: the line turns, and from the front the card looks narrower by the cosine of the turn.
key_points: Perpendicular to HP: TV is a line at $\phi$ to xy; perpendicular to VP: FV is a line at $\theta$
Stage 1: true shape in one view; stage 2: tilt the line view, project
Widths shorten by $\cos$ of the angle, heights stay true
Plane $\perp$ VP: VT is the FV line, HT is $\perp$ xy

questions.q: A square plate of 40 mm side is perpendicular to the HP and inclined at $30^\circ$ to the VP. One edge is perpendicular to the HP. Draw the projections and state the width in the front view.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Stage 1:** plate parallel to VP. FV is the true square 40 x 40 with one side vertical; TV is a line 40 mm long parallel to xy.

**Stage 2:** rotate the TV line through $30^\circ$ to xy about the end of the vertical edge. The TV is a line 40 mm long at $30^\circ$.

**FV:** project up from the new TV; heights stay 40 mm; the width becomes $40\cos30^\circ=34.64$ mm. The front view is a rectangle 34.64 x 40 mm.

subtopics.title: Edge on the HP: surface inclined to HP, edge inclined to VP
subtopics.theory_md:
Standard three-stage problem: a lamina has an edge in the HP, its surface at $\theta$ to HP and that edge at $\phi$ to VP.

1. **Stage 1:** lamina flat on HP, edge on xy (or $\parallel$ xy). TV = true shape; FV = line on xy.
2. **Stage 2:** tilt the FV about the resting edge to $\theta$. Project the TV (depths $\times\cos\theta$).
3. **Stage 3:** redraw the stage-2 TV with the edge at $\phi$ to xy. Project the FV: **heights stay as in stage 2**.

If instead the line from the edge mid-point (a perpendicular) is given in TV, rotate until that line makes the angle. Holes: plot by 8 to 12 points, they become ellipses. Heights stay, angles with HP stay.

subtopics.title: Corner on the HP: diagonal and surface angles
subtopics.theory_md:
A lamina resting on a **corner** in the HP, surface at $\theta$ to HP: the tilt axis is the line through the corner parallel to xy, so the **diagonal through that corner** is the line of greatest slope and is itself at $\theta$ to HP.

1. **Stage 1:** TV true shape, the diagonal through the resting corner $\perp$ xy; FV a line.
2. **Stage 2:** tilt the FV about the corner; the diagonal (length $D$) now has TV $D\cos\theta$ and the far corner height $D\sin\theta$; the other diagonal stays parallel to HP.
3. **Stage 3:** rotate the TV until the TV of the diagonal makes the given angle with xy; project the FV from stage-2 heights.

If the TV of the diagonal is already $\perp$ VP, there is no stage 3.
Square diagonal $=1.414\,s$; hexagon across corners $=2s$.

subtopics.theory_md:
Mirror of the HP case: interchange HP/VP, TV/FV and $\theta/\phi$.

subtopics.title: True and apparent shapes: circle, rectangle, rhombus
subtopics.theory_md:
When a plane is tilted by $\theta$ about a line parallel to xy, dimensions **perpendicular to the tilt line** shorten by $\cos\theta$ and dimensions along it stay true. So:

- A **circle** appears as an **ellipse**: major axis $=D$, minor axis $=D\cos\theta$.
- Area of the view $=$ true area $\times\cos\theta$.
- To make a view of a given shape (e.g. a square from a rectangle or rhombus), equate the shortened dimension to the needed dimension and solve for $\theta$.
- The axis along which the dimension stays true is the one parallel to both HP and VP.

Then draw stage 1 (flat), stage 2 (tilt), as usual.
subtopics.basics_md: Tilting a card only shrinks it in the direction it is tilting. The edge along the hinge keeps its length. So a shape can be turned into another shape by choosing the tilt.

Circle $\to$ ellipse with minor $=D\cos\theta$
Equate projected length to required length to find the angle

subtopics.title: Auxiliary planes: what they are and how a view is drawn
subtopics.theory_md:
An **auxiliary plane** gives a new view of an object to show a true length or true shape.

- **AVP** (auxiliary vertical plane): $\perp$ HP, inclined to VP. New reference line $x_1y_1$ is drawn in the **TV**; the new view is an **auxiliary elevation**: its heights from $x_1y_1$ equal the heights in the FV.
- **AIP** (auxiliary inclined plane): $\perp$ VP, inclined to HP. $x_1y_1$ is drawn in the **FV**; the **auxiliary plan** has distances from $x_1y_1$ equal to the distances in the TV.

Rule: draw projectors from the given view perpendicular to $x_1y_1$ and set off the dimension carried from the **other** view. A second auxiliary plane $\perp$ to the first gives a further view.
subtopics.basics_md: Walk around the object to a new standpoint. The new picture's up-and-down measurements are borrowed from the old picture that did not change direction.
key_points: AVP is $\perp$ HP: $x_1y_1$ in TV, heights from FV
AIP is $\perp$ VP: $x_1y_1$ in FV, distances from VP taken from TV
Projectors are perpendicular to $x_1y_1$
The new reference line is drawn parallel to a line to get its true length

4. Join the points in order; this is the auxiliary elevation.

subtopics.theory_md:
To find the **true length and $\theta$**: draw $x_1y_1$ **parallel to the top view** $ab$ (any distance). Auxiliary elevation $a_1'b_1'$: projectors $\perp x_1y_1$, heights from FV. Then $a_1'b_1'=TL$ and its angle with $x_1y_1$ is $\theta$.

To find **TL and $\phi$**: draw $x_1y_1$ **parallel to the front view** $a'b'$; auxiliary plan $a_1b_1=TL$, angle with $x_1y_1$ is $\phi$.

A second auxiliary plane $x_2y_2\perp a_1'b_1'$ shows the line as a **point**. A line is true length in the view whose reference line is parallel to the other view of it.

subtopics.title: True shape of a plane by auxiliary planes
subtopics.theory_md:
**Plane perpendicular to a reference plane** (a line in one view): draw $x_1y_1$ **parallel to that line** and project the other view across: the auxiliary view is the **true shape**.

**Oblique plane** (inclined to both): needs **two** auxiliary planes. First draw $x_1y_1$ perpendicular to the projectors so that one view becomes a line (take a line of the plane parallel to a reference plane; its true length is perpendicular to the projectors). The plane is then seen edge-on (a line). Second, draw $x_2y_2$ **parallel to that edge view**; the next view is the **true shape**.

Edge view first, then parallel: that is the entire method.
subtopics.basics_md: To see a card full face, you look straight at it, perpendicular to its surface. An edge view is a viewpoint in the plane of the card; turn 90 degrees from that and you face the card.
key_points: Plane $\perp$ HP or VP: $x_1y_1\parallel$ its line view gives true shape
Oblique plane: first get an edge view, then $x_2y_2\parallel$ edge view
Edge view uses a line of the plane parallel to a reference plane
Heights/distances are carried from the matching original view

questions.q: A square plate of 50 mm side is perpendicular to the VP and appears in the FV as a line 50 mm long at $30^\circ$ to xy. Find the TV width and show how to get the true shape with an auxiliary plane.
questions.model_answer_md:
The TV width is foreshortened: $50\cos30^\circ=43.30$ mm (the other dimension stays 50 mm), so the TV is a rectangle 50 x 43.30 mm.

**True shape:** draw $x_1y_1$ parallel to the FV line; draw projectors perpendicular to $x_1y_1$ from the FV points; take distances from the VP from the TV and set them off from $x_1y_1$. The auxiliary plan is the true square 50 x 50 mm.
points: TV width $50\cos30^\circ=43.30$ mm
$x_1y_1$ parallel to the FV line
Distances taken from the TV
